person.biography:
I am a biologist with an international PhD and a Master’s degree in Patient Advocacy. My research focuses on infection and inflammation in cystic fibrosis, integrating mouse models and clinical data to investigate pathogenic mechanisms affecting both pulmonary and extrapulmonary systems.
In collaboration with the Italian Cystic Fibrosis Foundation, I co-founded a state-of-the-art facility dedicated to preclinical models for testing innovative therapies, particularly anti-infective and anti-inflammatory approaches.
As a passionate patient advocate and EUPATI expert, I promote collaboration among scientists, patients, and stakeholders. I focus on advancing patient engagement in research, ensuring that diverse perspectives shape the direction and outcomes of research.

person.biography: Dr. Valerie Waters is a Senior Associate Scientist and Professor in the Division of Infectious Diseases, Department of Pediatrics. She is the infectious diseases consultant for the Cystic Fibrosis Clinic at SickKids and St Michael’s Hospital, as well as a CF researcher. Dr Waters' research program is focused on the investigation of the epidemiology and treatment of multi-drug resistant bacterial pathogens causing lung infections in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). She is particularly interested in the way these organisms grow as communities of bacteria known as biofilms, which are associated with increased antimicrobial resistance. The Waters Lab has developed novel biofilms models to test the efficacy of compounds against Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms, in the context of host factors and other microbes. They are currently studying the interaction between Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa grown within biofilms in the context of failure of early eradication treatment of P. aeruginosa in children with CF and in pulmonary exacerbations. In addition, the team has also recently conducted a clinical trial of oral prednisone as an adjuvant therapy in CF patients with pulmonary exacerbations.

person.biography: Wendy Unger is an associate professor at the Laboratory of Pediatrics, Erasmus MC – Sophia Children’s Hospital in Rotterdam, The Netherlands. She started her work on the biology of antigen-presenting cells (APCs), in the field of tumorimmunology and autoimmunity in Amsterdam (The Netherlands). Since 2015 she heads the Infection&Immunity group at Erasmus MC – Sophia Children’s Hospital. Here, she also had the first contact with Cystic Fibrosis. Her team investigates how APCs in the airways  interact with bacteria, how this results in specific T- and B-cell (memory) responses and how these processes are impacted by chronic inflammation. Her lab was important in clinical collaborations to analyze unique human material aiming to understand the pathogenesis of Cystic Fibrosis, where they demonstrated that crucial functions of APCs are affected.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) airway colonization in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) requires close monitoring due to its association with increased pulmonary exacerbations, progressive lung damage and accelerated decline in pulmonary function. Prior studies from our group identified pwCF who produced highly neutralizing antibodies against the type III secretion system (T3SS) of Pa. The aim of this work is to investigate the clinical relevance of these antibodies and immunological mechanisms driving chronic Pa infection.

Methods: We quantified serum T3SS-neutralizing activity in 99 pwCF and 12 healthy individuals. Neutralization capacity was integrated with immunophenotyping, including FACS-based characterization and bulk RNA sequencing of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), as well as clinical parameters. In the CF group, blood samples were collected twice with a time interval of two years.

Results: As expected, high neutralization capacity (Pa-Abhigh) was associated with chronic Pa infection. Immunophenotyping of pwCF with high and low neutralization revealed distinct cellular profiles including specific differences in monocyte and lymphocyte subpopulations, with more non-classical monocytes and fewer naïve CD8+ T-cells in Pa-Abhigh. These cellular alterations were reflected in transcriptomic differences, particularly within cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and adaptive immunity pathways. Spirometry data showed that Pa-Abhigh individuals had reduced forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). Moreover, an increase of Pa neutralization over time was linked to a progressive decline in FEV1.

Conclusion: Our findings offer a mechanistic insight into the development of potent neutralizing anti-T3SS antibodies and reveal a unique immunological profile linked to chronic Pa infection and reduced lung function. Incorporating this immune signature into clinical practice may enable early detection of patients at risk of disease progression.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa poses a major challenge in chronic airway disease, particularly in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Carbapenem-resistant P. aeruginosa is considered a highest-priority bacterial threat, with resistance frequently driven by loss-of-function mutations in the carbapenem uptake porin OprD. However, the broader consequences of these mutations for bacterial physiology and infection dynamics remain poorly understood.

Methods: Clinical P. aeruginosa strains isolated longitudinally from pwCF were analyzed to assess the emergence of oprD mutations. The effects of OprD loss were evaluated using an air–liquid interface airway epithelial model, measuring early bacterial attachment and translocation across epithelial barriers. Biophysical analyses were performed to assess changes in outer membrane properties and mucus interactions due to OprD loss across diverse clinical genomic backgrounds.

Results: Here we show that oprD mutations can arise in clinical strains isolated from pwCF in the absence of carbapenem treatment, suggesting selective pressures beyond direct antibiotic exposure. In the airway epithelial model, oprD mutants displayed enhanced early attachment to epithelial surfaces and increased translocation across the epithelial barrier, a phenotype conserved across diverse clinical genomic backgrounds. Biophysical analyses indicated that loss of OprD alters outer membrane charge and reduces mucus entrapment, thereby facilitating epithelial colonization independently of antimicrobial pressure.

Conclusion: These findings demonstrate that antibiotic resistance mutations can directly modulate host–pathogen interactions during airway infection, reshaping colonization dynamics beyond their impact on antibiotic susceptibility. This highlights the need to consider the wider biological effects of resistance-associated mutations when evaluating infection dynamics and clinical outcomes.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) causes chronic lung infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Small molecules known as modulators partially restore the defective protein causing CF. Despite several patients experience sputum load decreases and apparently resolve chronic bacterial infection, PA may persist through adaptation.

We investigated how PA adapts to the changed environment in pwCF during modulators therapy by integrating phenotypic and genomic data.

Methods: We investigated 563 PA strains isolated from 35 chronically colonised pwCF collected from a maximum of 15 years pre-treatment and up to 3 years post-treatment with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) or previous modulators. Phenotypic resistance and biofilm production under conditions mimicking the CF lung environment were confronted with Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) data to elucidate changes under modulators' selective pressure.

Results: 31 out of 35 pwCF retained the same Sequence Type (ST) pre-ETI, despite 1 case of prolonged negativity; 9 acquired new STs (even High-Risk Clones) without loss and 4 had clone replacement. Changes observed under modulators involved loss of non-mucoid morphotype, biofilm hyperproduction (up to 18-fold), and changes in antibiotic resistance. Hypermutability appeared under 3 different modulators (8 cases, ETI included) but decreased only under ETI (4 cases). Evolution of colonising PA into novel STs was also observed under ETI. Indeed, in 3 pwCF, ST274 evolved in novel STs, with convergent evolution giving rise to the same novel ST in 2 of them.

Conclusions: Our data indicate variability in the response to modulators, which drive adaptation through phenotypic and genomic changes with ambivalent effects, requiring attention in terms of their clinical implications. Some STs demonstrate reduced persistence in the face of pressure exerted by modulators. This suggests that modulator therapy could have a greater impact on lung colonisation in certain pwCF.

Objectives: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is a key pathogen in cystic fibrosis (CF), linked to high morbidity and mortality. Early antibiotic therapy may eradicate new PA, but if it reappears, eradication may not have happened. Distinguishing between strain persistence and new acquisition is crucial for guiding treatment strategies to prevent chronicity. This is also important for CF patients on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), re-presenting PA after negativity.

Using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), we aimed to assess the clonality of PA strains, focusing on isolates responsible for 1st and 2nd infections, intermittent colonisation and re-emergence on ETI.

Methods: A total of 103 PA isolates causing infection in 36 people with CF (pwCF) were compared by FTIR with post-treatment isolates. Two were chronically colonized and 2 intermittently colonised; 12 had a history of chronic colonization followed by PA negativity after starting modulator treatment; and 20 had received eradication therapy for a first PA infection, in 10 cases either before or after initiating modulators. Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) was used to validate FTIR results.

Results: FTIR and WGS revealed same-strain persistence in 24 patients, confirming a 100% predictive value for FTIR. Persistence occurred in intermittently and chronically colonised pwCF: 9 on modulators and 11 underwent eradication therapy (6 on modulators). WGS identified 3 FTIR misclassifications (3 pairs of isolates deemed as different), due to phenotypic differences and spectral variability among PA isolates. Significant temporal overlap between new infections and failed eradications demonstrates timing’s unreliability as sole differentiator.

Conclusions: FTIR is an easily implementable diagnostic tool that can define the success of eradicating therapy and optimise therapy. Our study proves its ability to inform appropriate therapeutic decisions for pwCF with recurrent PA infections.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: P. aeruginosa is a major pathogen in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, causing chronic lung infections associated with strong inflammation. In chronically infected patients, persistent P. aeruginosa form biofilm, which confers protection against host immunity and antibiotics, making infections refractory to treatments. In addition, co-infections with S. aureus are commonly observed in CF patients. To better control chronic infections, we developed a model in zebrafish embryo to study in vivo the bacterial persistence of clinical CF isolates in the context of mono or co-infections.

This work aims to characterize the host inflammatory response associated with persistent bacteria in the context of mono- or co-infections and to determine the localization of persistent bacteria in vivo, assessing whether they adopt a biofilm-like state.

Methods: Zebrafish embryos were infected using a wound infection method with CF isolates. Various fluorescent tools were used: il1b:GFP fish line to assess the inflammatory response, mfap4:mCherry fish line to assess the intra-macrophagic localization of bacteria by confocal microscopy, and a fluorescent biofilm reporter to assess a biofilm-like state of bacteria.

Results: We observed a strong il-1b response during persistent infection by P. aeruginosa CF isolates, which can be modulated in the context of co-infection with S. aureus (Costes et al., 2025). Persistent bacteria were visualized as intra-macrophagic clusters. Preliminary results showed the activation of a biofilm reporter for persistent P. aeruginosa.

Conclusion: The zebrafish embryo is a relevant and powerful in vivo model to study P. aeruginosa persistence in mono- and co-infection. Notably, we have translated main parts of our findings in mammalian models. The visualization of intracellular, biofilm-like bacterial aggregates, associated with a pro-inflammatory response paves the way to identify and test therapeutic strategies efficient against chronic infections.

records.affiliations_text: 1Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Biology and Biotechnology "Charles Darwin", Rome, Italy, 2Sapienza University of Rome, Department of Pediatrics and Infant Neuropsychiatry, Rome, Italy, 3San Gallicano Dermatological Institute IRCSS, Microbiology and Virology Unit, Rome, Italy
records.abstract_text:
Colistin, a last-resort antibiotic against multidrug resistant Gram-negative bacteria (doi:10.1189/fcimb.2022.851784), targets the bacterial outer membrane (OM) by electrostatic interactions. Bacteria may counteract this mechanism by OM remodeling which in P. aeruginosa is mainly due to lipid A aminoarabinosylation mediated by the arn operon. Based on previous observations showing that P. aeruginosa biofilms are tolerant to colistin (doi: 10.1371/journal.ppat.1000213), we asked whether the arn operon is involved in this phenomenon. For this, colistin MBIC (Minimal Biofilm Inhibition Concentration) and arn genes expression was analyzed in biofilms from colistin sensitive reference strains and cystic fibrosis clinical isolates, both wt and Darn mutants. Additionally, as P. aeruginosa experience a mild acidic environment in CF airways, in which it grows as a biofilm within the mucus, we tested whether pH changes the susceptibility to colistin in biofilms.

Our results showed higher arnT expression in biofilms as compared to planktonic cells, in agreement with higher biofilm resistance to colistin respect to the planktonic counterpart. In agreement with this finding, deletion of arn genes makes P. aeruginosa biofilms more susceptible to colistin. Similarly, blocking the arn operon activity with the ArnT inhibitors FDO and FDO-H (doi:10.1093/jac/dkaa200; 10.1021/acs.joc.0c01459) caused an MBIC reduction ranging from 128- to 8-fold in clinical isolates.

As expected, P. aeruginosa biofilms appeared more resistant to colistin at pH 6 respect to pH 7, with an increase of the colistin of MBIC ranging from 2- to 4-fold, depending on the strains.

Collectively, having confirmed the upregulation of the arn operon and the increased resistance to colistin of P. aeruginosa biofilms, our results support the use of ArnT inhibitors to potentiate colistin activity in the clinical settings in which biofilm-grown cells are prevalent, such as chronic lung infections.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Chronic infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) in the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF) is challenging to eradicate. Development of new drugs faces many barriers, so repurposing existing drugs is increasingly appealing. Our previous work showed the ability of glatiramer acetate (GA), an approved drug for use in multiple sclerosis, to synergise with tobramycin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, against clinical Pa from pwCF. This effect is likely due to antimicrobial peptide-like bacterial membrane damage. Here, we test the effect of GA addition to multiple classes of antibiotics to evaluate possible potentiation.

Methods: Thirty clinical Pa isolates from pwCF at the Royal Brompton Hospital were selected from the UK CF Infection Biorepository. Isolates represented various antimicrobial sensitivities and differing mucoid status. Checkerboard assays assessed the effect of two concentrations of GA on the growth inhibitory impact of clinically relevant antibiotics.

Results: Addition of 200 µg/ml GA significantly reduced the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC50) of aminoglycosides amikacin (p<0.001, n=11) and gentamicin (p=0.001, n=12) for 100% of isolates tested, of which 64% and 60% were sensitive to gentamicin and amikacin respectively.

Preliminary data indicated a strain-specific variability of GA's potentiation with the antibiotics aztreonam, ciprofloxacin, piperacillin/tazobactam, ceftazidime and colistin (n=10). GA does not potentiate meropenem (n=10). Further isolates are being screened and data will be available for the conference.

Conclusion: GA shows an extended ability to potentiate other aminoglycosides against antibiotic sensitive and resistant Pa. The effect of GA on non-aminoglycoside agents varies, which may aid exploration of the incompletely understood mechanism of action of GA. These results enhances evidence of the promising effect of GA with antimicrobial treatments in pwCF.

records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in people with cystic fibrosis feature persistent inflammation and oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms enabling bacterial persistence remain unclear. We investigated whether mutations in the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHc) drive pyruvate secretion that promotes persistence, and whether analogous mutations occur in other airway pathogens.

Methods: We analyzed clinical isolates by comparative genomics to identify PDHc mutations, quantified extracellular pyruvate, and used airway epithelial cell at the air-liquid interface and macrophage infection models to assess host responses. We tested oxidative‑stress scavenging (H₂O₂), immune‑activation readouts, and phagocytosis survival to determine functional consequences of pyruvate secretion.

Results: Clinical P. aeruginosa isolates harbored PDHc mutations that increased pyruvate secretion, establishing a more tolerogenic infection microenvironment and favoring bacterial persistence. Pyruvate scavenged reactive oxygen species (H₂O₂), dampened immune activation in epithelial cells and macrophages, and enhanced bacterial survival during phagocytosis. Analogous mutations were also identified in Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.

Conclusion: Pyruvate functions as a bacterial immunometabolite that mimics host antioxidant defenses, reshaping the infection niche to enable long‑term colonization, consistent with the concept of disease tolerance. These findings highlight secreted metabolites as key mediators of host–pathogen interactions and suggest therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic pathways to manage chronic infections.

records.title: The role of gyrA and gyrB mutations in the adaptation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa to cystic fibrosis airways
records.authors_text: E. Cebrián-Sastre1, P. Laborda1, A.M. Rudjord-Levann1, R. La Rosa1,2, S. Molin3, H.K. Johansen1,2,4
records.affiliations_text: 1Rigshospitalet, Department of Clinical Microbiology, Copenhagen, Denmark, 2Technical University of Denmark, Department of Health Technology, Kongens Lyngby, Denmark, 3The Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Biosustainability, Technical University of Denmark, Kongens Lyngby, Denmark, 4University of Copenhagen, Department of Clinical Medicine, Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences, Copenhagen, Denmark
records.abstract_text:
Objectives: Mutations in gyrA and gyrB, encoding the two subunits of a type II topoisomerase, are frequently detected in clinical isolates of Pseudomonas aeruginosa from people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). This study aims to explore how mutations in these genes contribute to bacterial adaptation during chronic lung infection.

Methods: We generated a panel of single gyrA and gyrB mutants using CRISPR-Cas9, representing pathoadaptive mutations commonly identified in clinical isolates. The ciprofloxacin (CIP) minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was determined in Mueller–Hinton medium using the broth microdilution method. The impact of these mutations during infection was investigated using air–liquid interface (ALI) models that closely mimic the cystic fibrosis (CF) airway environment, both in the absence and presence of antibiotic pressure.

Results: Mutations in gyrA and gyrB are commonly associated with CIP resistance. Interestingly, we observed that not all mutations identified in isolates from pwCF lead to an increased CIP MIC. This suggests that some of these mutations may play additional roles beyond antibiotic resistance, potentially contributing to host adaptation, affecting bacterial fitness, or acting as compensatory changes.

Conclusions: Overall, this work improves our understanding of the role of gyrA and gyrB mutations in the adaptation of P. aeruginosa during CF airway infection. These insights may have clinical relevance by helping to predict bacterial evolutionary trajectories and optimise treatment strategies, ultimately supporting more personalised therapeutic approaches.

records.authors_text: P. Gierlich1, A. de Bruijn1, I. Boon1, P. Croughs2, H.M Janssens3, W.W. Unger1
records.affiliations_text: 1Erasmus MC-Sophia Children’s Hospital, Pediatrics, Laboratory of Pediatrics, Rotterdam, Netherlands, 2Erasmus MC-Sophia Children’s Hospital, Medical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases, Rotterdam, Netherlands, 3Erasmus MC-Sophia Children’s Hospital, Pediatrics, Division of Respiratory Medicine and Allergology, Rotterdam, Netherlands
records.abstract_text:
Objective: Chronic airway infections caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) remain a substantial burden for people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). The persistent chronic infection and the alarming rise in antibiotic resistance make Pa difficult to treat, highlighting the urgency for alternative treatment strategies. Non-digestible oligosaccharides (NDOs) have emerged as promising compounds with antimicrobial properties.

Aim: To investigate the antimicrobial activity of the NDOs chito- and alginate-oligosaccharides (COS and AOS) against both antibiotic-resistant and -sensitive Pa strains.

Methods and results: Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC), Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC), and time-kill kinetic (TKK) assays demonstrated that COS and AOS inhibited growth and killed antibiotic sensitive and resistant Pa in a concentration-dependent manner within 24h. Adding COS to ceftazidime or tobramycin or AOS to ceftazidime, reduced the required antibiotic concentration 4- to 8-fold, restoring antibiotic efficacy in clinical isolates and shifting resistant strains into a susceptible range (MIC 16  2 µg/ml). In an in vitro lung infection model, 2% COS and 4% AOS prevented Pa attachment and internalization without cytotoxicity to respiratory epithelium, while 2% COS alone and in combination with tobramycin eradicated intracellular Pa. Mechanistic studies showed that COS, but not AOS, disrupted bacterial membrane integrity, explaining its antibiotic-potentiating effect. Neither of the NDOs promoted resistance development within 7 days of incubation, yet they maintained antimicrobial activity in artificial sputum medium (ASM).

Conclusions: COS and AOS are both promising new antimicrobials against Pa, that act synergistically with existing antibiotics, restoring antibiotic sensitivity in resistant strains.

person.title: Dr.
person.biography: Wendy Unger is an associate professor at the Laboratory of Pediatrics, Erasmus MC – Sophia Children’s Hospital in Rotterdam, The Netherlands. She started her work on the biology of antigen-presenting cells (APCs), in the field of tumorimmunology and autoimmunity in Amsterdam (The Netherlands). Since 2015 she heads the Infection&Immunity group at Erasmus MC – Sophia Children’s Hospital. Here, she also had the first contact with Cystic Fibrosis. Her team investigates how APCs in the airways  interact with bacteria, how this results in specific T- and B-cell (memory) responses and how these processes are impacted by chronic inflammation. Her lab was important in clinical collaborations to analyze unique human material aiming to understand the pathogenesis of Cystic Fibrosis, where they demonstrated that crucial functions of APCs are affected.
